title: Effects of atorvastatin and/or probucol on recovery of atherosclerosis in high-fat-diet-fed apolipoprotein E-deficient mice.

Original article
Eﬀects of atorvastatin and/or probucol on recovery of atherosclerosis in
high-fat-diet-fed apolipoprotein E–deﬁcient mice
Xiaokun Guoa, Lin Wanga, Xiaoshuang Xiab, Peilu Wangb, Xin Lia,⁎
a Department of Geratology, The Second Hospital of Tianjin Medical University, PR China
b Department of Neurology, The Second Hospital of Tianjin Medical University, PR China
A R T I C L E I N F O
Keywords:
Atherosclerosis
Atorvastatin
Probucol
Endoplasmic reticulum stress
TLR-4
NF-κB
A B S T R A C T
Introduction: We have investigated the possible eﬀects and mechanism of atorvastatin, a statin, and/or probucol,
a powerful antioxidant used to lower cholesterol before 1995, on the atherosclerosis development.
Methods: Apolipoprotein-E-deﬁcient (ApoE−/−) mice fed with the high fat diet were randomly divided into 3
groups (n = 10/each group): Placebo, Atorvastatin (10 mg/ kg/d), and atorvastatin (10 mg/kg/d) plus probucol
(10 mg/kg/d) groups. C57BL/6 J mice were fed with normal diet as the control group (n = 10). Animals were
sacriﬁced 10 weeks after the intervention. To evaluate the experimental atherosclerosis, blood tests were used
for measuring serum lipoprotein proﬁle, Western blots for endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress protein expression,
H&E staining for plaque lesions, immunohistology for macrophages, inﬂammatory cytokines, innate immune
receptor TLR-4, transcription factor NF-κB, and atherosclerosis plaques.
Results: Compared with the control group, ApoE−/−mice in the placebo group showed with the signiﬁcantly
(p < 0.05) higher levels of serum total cholesterol (TC), triglyceride (TG), low-density lipoprotein cholesterol
(LDL) and oxidized low density lipoprotein (ox-LDL), PERK, GRP78, CHOP, IL-1β, TNF-α and NF-κB, but with
the lower levels of high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (HDL) and TLR-4, and also the increase in macrophages
and the aortic media collagen, and the decrease in the elastic ﬁbers (p < 0.01). Treatment with atorvastatin
recovered all these features (p < 0.05 or p < 0.01) near to the levels in the control group. In addition, the
combination of atorvastatin and probucol has shown the slightly stronger eﬀect than the use of atorvastatin
alone without statistical signiﬁcances when comparing most bio-markers of atherosclerosis, but with signiﬁcant
diﬀerences in the reduction of the plaque lesion areas and macrophages (p < 0.05).
Conclusions: Atorvastatin and/or probucol suppresses ER stress and increase the level of TLR-4, which lowers
NF-κB, resulting in the recovery of atherosclerosis in the ApoE−/−mouse model.
1. Introduction
As a leading cause of death in many countries, including China,
atherosclerosis has been linked to hypercholesterolemia that char-
acterized by a high level of circulating low-density lipoprotein choles-
terol (LDL) [1]. Endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress has been reportedly
participated in the pathogenesis of atherosclerosis, heart failure and
other cardiovascular diseases by activating C/EBP homologous protein
(CHOP)-mediated apoptosis and inﬂammation, which stabilizes ather-
osclerotic plaques [2–4]. In the process of atherosclerosis, levels of
serum pro-inﬂammatory cytokines, including interleukin 1 (IL1β) and
tumor necrosis factor (TNF-α), unsurely increase [5,6].
Apolipoprotein-E (ApoE) is an important modulator of many stages
of lipoprotein metabolism [7,8]. Although it is mainly synthesized in
the liver and brain, ApoE is also expressed in vessels and may have local
eﬀects on cholesterol homeostasis and on inﬂammatory reactions in
atherosclerotic vessels [9]. The ApoE-deﬁcient (ApoE−/−) mouse line is
a well-established genetic animal model of atherosclerotic hypercho-
lesterolemia, in which mice spontaneously develop hypercholester-
olemia and atherosclerosis on chow diet [10].
Statins, including atorvastatin, are a class of drugs which exhibit a
powerful hypocholesterolemic eﬀect, as revolutionized cholesterol-
lowing agents. Treatment with statins has been reported to markedly
reduce morbidities and mortalities of major cardiovascular events in
patients [11,12]. A powerful antioxidant, probucol, inhibits the oxi-
dation of cholesterol in LDLs, which slows the formation of foam cells
that contribute to atherosclerotic plaques [13]. Although clinical trials
were stopped after it was found that lower HDL in patients with a

previous history of heart disease [14], probucol has been investigated

In this study, we have used ApoE−/−mice as animal models to
investigate the eﬀects of atorvastatin and/or probucol on hypercho-
lesterolemia in atherosclerosis. In addition, we have investigated the
possible mechanism, including changes of ER stress signaling, pro-in-
ﬂammatory cytokines and the regulation between TLR-4 and NF-κB.
2. Materials and methods
2.1. Animals and treatment
All animal experiments were performed in compliance with the
National Standard on Laboratory Animal Welfare and Ethics of China
(Draft, 2016) and conform to NIH guidelines. Ten male C57BL/6 J mice
at the age of 8 weeks were adaptive feeding on a normal chow diet as
the control (C) group. Thirty male ApoE knockout (ApoE−/−) mice in
C57BL/6 J background (Jackson Lab, USA) at the age of 8 weeks were
adaptive feeding on a normal chow diet for 1 week and placed on high-
fat diet (78.8% standard diet, 10.0% yolk powder, 10.0% lard, 1.0%
cholesterol, and 0.2% sodium taurocholate) for 10 weeks. The mice
were randomly divided into 3 groups (n = 10/group). Mice were orally
gavaged with placebo dissolved in ultrapure water in the placebo (P)
group, atorvastatin (Pﬁzer, NY, USA) (10 mg/kg/d) in the atorvastatin
(A) group, and atorvastatin (10 mg/kg/d) plus probucol (10 mg/kg/d)
in the atorvastatin plus probucol (A + Pr) group for 10 weeks. At the
end of the treatment period, all animals were fasted overnight. Mice
were anesthetized by intraperitoneal injection with 10% chloral hy-
drate (350 mg/kg), following eyeball extirpation to collect the blood.
Aortic tissues were harvested, ﬁxed in 4% paraformaldehyde in phos-
phate buﬀered saline (PBS), and embedded in paraﬃn for histological
analysis. Some aortic tissues were obtained and kept frozen in liquid
nitrogen immediately, and then stored at −80 °C for western blot.
2.2. Serum lipoprotein proﬁle
The blood samples were collected and serum was prepared by
centrifugation at 3500 rpm for 15 min. Following the manufactural in-
struction, Total Cholesterol Assay Kit (COD-PAP method) (Nanjing
Jiancheng Biological Technology Institute, China) was used for de-
tecting serum total cholesterol (TC), and Triglyceride Assay Kit (GPO-
PAP method) (Nanjing Jiancheng Biological Technology Institute,
China) for triglyceride (TG), HDL/LDL Assay Kit (Beijing Chongyu
Biological Technology Co., Ltd.) for high-density lipoprotein cholesterol
(HDL) and low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL). The serum oxLDL
levels were analyzed using Mouse Oxidized Low Density Lipoprotein
(ox-LDL) ELISA Kit (Shanghai Beinuo Biological Technology Co. Ltd.) as
a marker of oxidative stress.
2.3. Western blot analysis
Aortas from all mice in diﬀerent groups were homogenized in lysis
buﬀer containing 10 mM Tris pH 7.4, 250 mM saccharose, 1 mM EDTA
and protease inhibitor cocktail (Roche, Germany). The homogenates
were centrifuged at 2500 rpm for 10 min and 10,000 rpm for 30 min at
4 °C. After determination of protein concentration in the supernatant by
the BCA™Protein Assay Kit (Pierce, Rockford, IL), samples (30 μg
protein)
were electrophoresed
on 12% SDS-polyacrylamide
gels.
Proteins were transferred to
Immu-Blot Membranes for Protein Blotting (Bio-Rad, CA, USA).
After blocking of non-speciﬁc binding sites in 5% non-fat dry milk,
membranes were incubated with the primary antibodies against phos-
phorylated protein kinase RNA (PKR)-like ER kinase (PERK), glucose-
regulated protein 78 (GRP78), (Santa Cruz, CA, USA), and C/EBP
homologous protein (CHOP) (Cell Signaling, MA, USA), and β-actin
(Abcam, MA, USA) overnight at 4 °C, and then with corresponding
secondary horseradish peroxidase-conjugated antibodies for 60 min at
room temperature, followed by the kit of SuperSignal West Pico
Chemiluminescent Substrate (Thermo, IL, USA). The membranes were
exposed using ChemiDoc MP Imaging System (Bio-Rad, CA, USA). To
quantify the bands of interest, the QuantityOne imaging software (Bio-
Rad) was used.
2.4. Histological analysis
Paraﬃn-embedded aorta tissues were cut into 5 μm-thick cross-
sections and deparaﬃnized prior to staining using a standard protocol.
Hematoxylin and eosin staining was used to for detecting the lesion
area at the aortic sinus, Sirius red staining for detecting collagen and
Orcein staining for elastic ﬁbers. Immunohistochemical staining was
performed according to the manufacture's description (Zsbio, Beijing,
China) with the antibody against macrophages (Abcam, MA, USA),
interleukin-1β (IL-1β), tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α), nuclear factor
kappa-light-chain-enhancer of activated B cells (NF-κB) or Toll-like
receptor 4 (TLR-4) (Santa Cruz, CA, USA). NIH Image J software was
used for quantiﬁcation.
2.5. Statistics
An ANOVA test was applied to assess the relationship between
diﬀerent variables where appropriate. An ANOVA test was applied to
deﬁne a diﬀerence among the diﬀerent treatment groups, which was
followed by a post-hoc multiple comparisons test to deﬁne speciﬁc
group
diﬀerences,
using
GraphPad
(Prism)
software.
Values
of
p < 0.05 were considered signiﬁcant and p < 0.01 very signiﬁcant.
3. Results
3.1. Eﬀects of atorvastatin and/or probucol on serum lipid levels
To study the eﬀect of Endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress and ator-
vastatin on atherosclerosis development, ApoE−/−mice with the
C57BL/6 J background were fed with the high fat diet with or without
atorvastatin and/or probucol for 10 weeks. C57BL/6 J mice fed with the
normal diet as the control. The levels of the serum lipids were mea-
sured. ANOVA followed by a post-hoc multiple comparisons test was
used determine whether signiﬁcant diﬀerences in diﬀerent treatment
groups and each two speciﬁc groups. The serum levels of total choles-
terol (TC) (p = 0.000 in the 4 group comparison) was 11.28 ± 0.9
mmol/L in the control (C) group, increased to 15.30 ± 1.23 mmol/L in
the placebo (P) group (p < 0.01, when compared with C group, de-
creased to 13.26 ± 1.06 mmol/L in the atorvastatin (A) group
(p < 0.01 when compared with P group) and 13.14 ± 1.24 mmol/L in
the atorvastatin plus probucol (A+Pr) group (p < 0.01, when com-
pared with P group, and p > 0.05, when compared with A group)
(Fig. 1A). The level of serum triglyceride (TG) (p = 0.000) was
1.83 ± 0.15 mmol/L in C group, signiﬁcantly increased to 2.43 ± 0.30
mmol/L in P group (p < 0.01, compared with C group), but sig-
niﬁcantly decreased to 1.95 ± 0.23 and 1.90 ± 0.18 mmol/L in A and
A+Pr groups (p < 0.01, compared with P group) (Fig. 1B). The level
of serum low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL) (p = 0.000) was
2.33 ± 0.31 mmol/L in C group, signiﬁcantly increased to 3.09 ± 0.28
mmol/L in P group (p < 0.01, compared with C group), but sig-
niﬁcantly decreased to 2.39 ± 0.38 and 2.36 ± 0.29 mmol/L in A and
A+Pr groups (p < 0.01, compared with P group) (Fig. 1C). The level
of serum high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (HDL) (p = 0.000) was
1.05 ± 0.11 mmol/L in C group, signiﬁcantly decreased to 0.83 ± 0.17
mmol/L in P group (p < 0.05, compared with C), but signiﬁcantly
increased to 1.03 ± 0.14 (p < 0.05, compared with P group) and
1.09 ± 0.19 mmol/L (p < 0.01, compared with P group) in A and
A+Pr groups (Fig. 1D). The data indicate that the high-fat diet

atorvastatin and/or probul treatment led to a signiﬁcant reduction in
the level of ox-LDL in ApoE-/- mice. Therefore, our results indicate the
eﬀects of these two chemicals on improving the conditions of athero-
sclerosis. The data also indicate that the combination treatment with
atorvastatin plus probul had more eﬀects than the used of only ator-
vastatin on the recovery of atherosclerosis, although without the
statistical diﬀerence.
3.2. Atorvastatin and/or probucol decrease endoplasmic reticulum (ER)
stress
Western blots using aorta samples showed that the level changes of
ER stress associated proteins in the diﬀerent groups. By normalizing the
protein expressing bands to β-actin and setting the protein expression
levels in C group as 1-fold, the levels of PERK, GRP78 and CHOP were
1.81 ± 0.27, 1.53 ± 0.12, 1.80 ± 0.11 in. P group, 1.37 ± 0.08,
1.18 ± 0.12, 1.33 ± 0.14 in. A group and 1.27 ± 0.13, 1.14 ± 0.03,
1.32 ± 0.14 in. A + Pr group, respectively. There were signiﬁcant
diﬀerences between P and C (p < 0.01), A (p < 0.05) or A+Pr
(p < 0.05) groups, but no signiﬁcant diﬀerences between C, A and
A+Pr groups (p > 0.05) (Fig. 2). The data suggest that the high fat

3.4. Atorvastatin and/or probucol downregulate NF-κB by the increase in
the TLR-4 level
As a protein complex, NF-κB controls transcription of DNA, cytokine
production and cell survival. Immunohistological staining showed that
the number of IL-1β positive cells was 19.8 ± 5.9% in C group, in-
creased to 30.4 ± 3.0% in P group (p < 0.01), and then decreased to
24.6 ± 2.8% (p < 0.05) and 23.5 ± 3.5% (p < 0.01) in A and A+Pr
groups (Fig. 3C), suggesting that atorvastatin and/or probucol down-
regulate NF-κB. On the other hand, the number of TLR-4 positive cells
was 23.0 ± 2.0% in C group, decreased to 16.3 ± 3.1% in P group
(p < 0.01), and then increased to 32.7 ± 4.9% (p < 0.05) and
30.3 ± 8.6% (p < 0.01) in A and A+Pr groups (Fig. 3D), suggesting
that atorvastatin and/or probucol attenuates NF-κB via. the increase in
TLR-4.
3.5. Atorvastatin and/or probucol reduce the lesion area at the aortic sinus
and plaque macrophages
H&E staining showed the lesion area at the aortic sinus (n = 10/
each group) (Fig. 4A). No lesion area had been observed in C group. The
average
lesion
area
was
0.291 ± 0.031
mm2
in
P
group,
0.145 ± 0.016 mm2 in A group and 0.123 ± 0.014 mm2 in A + Pr
group (p = 0.000 in the 4 group comparison; p < 0.05 between A and
A+Pr groups, and p < 0.01 between other each two groups) (Fig. 4A).
Macrophages were stained brown by immunohistological staining
(Fig. 4B). Quantiﬁcation of macrophages was 21.4 ± 3.8 in C group,
increased to 33.5 ± 4.4 in. P group, and then decreased to 25.7 ± 3.6
and 22.3 ± 2.2 in. A and A + Pr groups (p = 0.000 in the 4 group
comparison; p < 0.05 between A and A+Pr groups, and p < 0.01
between other each two groups) (Fig. 4B). The data suggest that ptor-
vastatin and/or probucol reduce the lesion area at the aortic sinus and
plaque macrophages, and the combination administration of atorvas-
tatin and probucol results in the stronger eﬀects than the use of ator-
vastatin alone with signiﬁcant diﬀerences (p < 0.05).
3.6. Aortic media collagen was reduced by atorvastatin and/or probucol
Sirius-red staining demonstrated an increased amount of interstitial
ﬁbrosis in the aortic media of ApoE−/−mice fed with the high fat diet
in P group (12.34 ± 1.56%) compared with C57BL/6 J mice fed with
the normal diet in C group (18.75 ± 2.31%) with signiﬁcant diﬀerence
(p < 0.01). Collagen content was signiﬁcantly lower after treatment
with atorvastatin (15.27 ± 1.39%) in A group and atorvastatin plus
probucol (14.45 ± 1.26%) (p < 0.05 and p < 0.01) in A+Pr group
(Fig. 5A, B, E). The data suggest that the high fat diet increases but
atorvastatin and/or probucol decreases aortic media collagen.

4. Discussion
Apolipoprotein E-deﬁcient (ApoE−/−) mice has been documented
as an animal model to develop marked hypercholesterolemia with a
prominent increase in the level of LDL and a decrease in the level of
HDL [17]. In our experiments, by feeding ApoE-/- mice with the high fat
diet we have established the animal model of atherosclerosis. By
comparison with C57BL/6 mice fed with the normal diet, the high fat
diet caused hypercholesterolemia with higher serum levels of total
cholesterol (TC), triglyceride (TG), low-density lipoprotein cholesterol
(LDL) and oxidized low-density lipoprotein (ox-LDL) but the lower level
of serum high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (HDL) (Fig. 1). The higher
levels of PERK, GRP78 and CHOP suggest the increase in the en-
doplasmic reticulum (ER) stress (Fig. 2). We have also observed the
increase in inﬂammatory cytokines IL-1β and TNF-α, and in the level of
transcription factor NF-κB accompanied with the lower level of TLR-4,
which indicate the inﬂammation induced by the higher level of ER
stress (Fig. 3). Hypercholesterolemia, ER stress, inﬂammatory cytokines
and transcription factor result in stabilizing atherosclerotic plaques
characteristics of increasing macrophages (Fig. 4), interstitial collagen
content and decreasing elastic ﬁbers (Fig. 5).
In this study, we have found the improvable eﬀects of atorvastatin,
one of stains, on atherosclerosis in the ApoE−/−mouse model.
Atorvastatin decreases the levels of TC, TG, LDL and oxLDL, and in-
creases HDL, to improve hypercholesterolemia (Fig. 1). It also decreases
the levels of ER stress proteins, PERK, GRP78 and CHOP (Fig. 2), and
inﬂammatory cytokines, IL-1β and TNF-α (Fig. 3), to nearly normal
levels. Especially, atorvastatin enhances the TLR-4 level resulting in the
lower level of the transcription factor NF-κB, which improves the
condition of atherosclerosis (Fig. 3). These eﬀects result in the decrease
in the plaque lesion areas, macrophages, interstitial collagen content
and elastic ﬁbers in aorta tissues (Figs. 4 and 5). The data are similar to
the research in a rabbit model [18].
Probucol is a potent antioxidative drug that has been used for pre-
vention and treatment of atherosclerotic cardiovascular diseases as a
lipid-lowering drug [19,20]. Western countries quitted its use in 1995
because of the reduction in serum HDL cholesterol. Recent researches
have shown that probucol enhances plasma cholesteryl ester transfer
protein activity and hepatic scavenger receptor class B type I, causing a
decrease in HDL-C, and accelerates the antioxidative function of HDL
via increase in paraoxonase 1 activity [21]. Combined using atorvas-
tatin and probucol, we have observed the slightly stronger eﬀects on
atherosclerosis when compared with the use of atorvastatin alone, with
no statistical signiﬁcance in the most bio-markers (Figs. 1, 2, 3 and 5).
When measuring the plaque lesion areas and macrophages, we have
found the combined using atorvastatin and probucol had more eﬀects
than use of atorvastatin alone with signiﬁcant diﬀerences (Fig. 4). A
similar research has been done in a rabbit model, in which probucol has
signiﬁcant add-on anti-atherosclerotic eﬀects when combined with
atorvastatin treatment [22]. Therefore, probucol might be considered
as an option in case statins are not eﬀective.
5. Conclusions
By using a APOE−/−mouse model, we have provided the evidence
that atorvastatin has eﬀects on the recovery of atherosclerosis by im-
proving hypercholesterolemia, suppressing ER stress and inﬂammatory
cytokines IL-1β and TNF-α, and increasing TLR-4 that downregulates
NF-κB. Combination of atorvastatin and probucol has slightly add-on
anti-atherosclerotic eﬀects when compared with the use of atorvastatin
alone without statistical signiﬁcance in the most bio-markers.
